title: Enhancing secondary school students' attitudes toward physics by using computer simulations
venue: International Journal of Data and Network Science
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether computer simulations can improve secondary school students’ attitudes toward physics, particularly attitudes toward scientific inquiry, enjoyment of science lessons, and interest in science-related careers. The authors frame the study as a response to concerns about negative attitudes toward physics and the need for more interactive science instruction.

The intervention used PhET interactive simulations of Newton’s Second Law of Motion in an eleventh-grade physics unit. Students in the experimental group completed simulation-based inquiry activities, while the control group received conventional face-to-face instruction and hands-on experiments. The study used a pre-test/post-test quasi-experimental design with 90 Grade 11 students from two public schools in Al Ain, United Arab Emirates, and measured attitudes using selected TOSRA scales.

Results showed statistically significant post-test differences favoring the simulation group on all three attitude dimensions: attitudes toward scientific inquiry, enjoyment of science lessons, and career interest in physics/science. The authors also reported large effect sizes and gender-related differences, with the simulation-based approach benefiting both male and female students. They conclude that computer simulations can meaningfully strengthen students’ attitudes toward physics and recommend wider integration of simulations into physics teaching, along with teacher training and further longitudinal research.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test control-group study with 90 secondary students and appropriate comparison groups, giving it moderate credibility. It is not randomized and relies on attitude outcomes rather than direct achievement, so it does not meet blue-tier standards.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported group effects are very large (e.g., t=22.76; partial η² values around .75-.80 across key subscales), indicating substantial impact on the measured attitude outcomes. The intervention targets a priority K-12 science population and shows strong positive effects.

interventions.use_case: PhET interactive computer simulation used as an inquiry tool to teach Newton’s Second Law of Motion in 11th-grade physics, replacing conventional face-to-face instruction and hands-on lab work with simulation-based virtual experiments.

finding.finding_summary: The study found statistically significant improvements in students’ attitudes toward science-related learning after the PhET simulation intervention. On the full TOSRA-related attitude measure, the experimental group (n=45) outperformed the control group (n=45) at post-test, t(88)=22.76, p=.000, with much higher mean scores (EG M=4.17, SD=.18 vs CG M=2.68, SD=.39).
finding.measure: TOSRA attitude scales, including attitudes toward scientific inquiry, enjoyment of science lessons, and career interest in science/physics

finding.finding_summary: The simulation-based group showed significant gains on the TOSRA Attitudes toward Scientific Inquiry scale. Post-test scores favored the experimental group (M=4.01, SD=.34) over the control group (M=2.49, SD=.54), with t(88)=15.819, p=.000 and a large multivariate group effect (partial η²=.748 for ASI in the group comparison).
finding.measure: TOSRA Attitudes toward Scientific Inquiry (ASI) scale

finding.finding_summary: The intervention improved students’ enjoyment of science lessons. The experimental group scored much higher than the control group on ESL post-test means (EG M=4.24, SD=.33 vs CG M=2.72, SD=.48), with t(88)=17.169, p=.000 and a large group effect in the MANOVA/ANOVA results (partial η²=.785).
finding.measure: TOSRA Enjoyment of Science Lessons (ESL) scale

finding.finding_summary: The PhET-based condition also improved career interest in physics/science. Post-test CIS scores favored the experimental group (EG M=4.26, SD=.29) over the control group (CG M=2.85, SD=.43), with t(88)=18.067, p=.000 and a large group effect (partial η²=.797).
finding.measure: TOSRA Career Interest in Science/Physics (CIS) scale
